description.narrative: Legal Resources Foundation har ansökt om 35 000 000 SEK som kärnstöd till Access to Justice Programme. Insatsmålen är följande: 1) Ökad tillgång till rättsskipning för marginaliserade och utsatta genom tillhandahållande av juridisk hjälp. 2) Att stärka marginaliserade och utsatta personers förmåga att hävda sina rättigheter genom tillhandahållande av information samt genom att utbilda samhällsadvokater och juridiska rådgivare som kan öka medvetenheten i lokala samhällen. 3) Bidra till en möjliggörande miljö där demokratiska rättigheter hävdas av en informerad allmänhet som kräver skydd och efterlevnad av konstitutionella och mänskliga rättigheter. 4) Ett effektivt och ansvarsfullt leveranssystem 5) Ökad tillgång till och förståelse för juridisk information.

The Legal Resources Foundation has applied for SEK 35 000 000, which is core support towards its Access to Justice Programme. The interventions objectives are as follows: 1) Increasing access to justice for the marginalized and vulnerable through the provision of legal assistance. 2) Strengthening the capacity of the marginalized and vulnerable to assert their rights through the provision of information as well as training community paralegals and peer legal advisors who can raise awareness in communities. 3) Contributing to an enabling environment where democratic rights are claimed by an informed public that demands the protection and enforcement of constitutional and human rights. 4) An efficient and accountable justice delivery system 5) Increased access to and understanding legal information.

sector.narrative: Justice, law and order policy, planning and administration

description.narrative:
The Legal Resources Foundation (LRF) implemented the Access to Justice (A2J) programme to enhance justice delivery for marginalized and vulnerable communities across Zimbabwe from January 2020 to August 2025. Through a combination of legal aid, policy advocacy, institutional capacitybuilding, and community engagement, the programme achieved systemic and sustainable improvements within both formal and customary justice systems. Its operations led to expanded coverage, responsive services, and measurable justice outcomes, assisting 31,253 new clients (11,476 men and 19,777 women), resolving 2,518 cases by lawyers and 25,872 by paralegals, and enabling 20,854 people to act as selfactors. These results demonstrate a clear difference: more people accessed timely remedies, more cases were concluded, and more communities were equipped to demand accountability. Overall, the interventions strengthened accountability, inclusivity, and gender responsiveness across key justice institutions while empowering citizens to actively claim and defend their rights.
Strengthening Institutional and Policy Frameworks A major achievement of the programme was the strengthening of institutional and policy frameworks that support access to justice. LRFs collaboration with the Zimbabwe Prisons and Correctional Service (ZPCS) resulted in a formal Memorandum of Understanding that institutionalized joint prison visits. Operationally, this led to 663 prison visits reaching 2,396 inmates (1,957 men and 439 women), and 1,501 juveniles receiving legal support. What changed within correctional facilities was not only procedure but also professional culture: officers adopted rehabilitative and rightsbased practices aligned with constitutional standards, improving bail facilitation, humane treatment, and protections for special groups such as nursing mothers and persons with mental health challenges. Attitudes and behaviours shifted towards gender sensitivity and childfriendly approaches, with immediate referrals of juvenile cases to LRF preventing unnecessary detention. At the community level, traditional leaderssupported by 83 traditional court monitoring sessions across 1,754 casesintegrated human rights principles in customary adjudication, which changed relations between citizens and customary authorities by building trust and ensuring more consistent, documented outcomes. Target groups that previously faced opaque or intimidating traditional processes could now approach these forums with confidence, secure in the knowledge of fairer, rightsaware adjudication. These operations made a tangible difference, evidenced by improved documentation, stronger procedural fairness, and sustained institutional collaboration through the MoU.
Modernizing Service Delivery Models The programme transformed access to justice by modernizing service delivery. The establishment of a tollfree call centre provided an innovative telejustice platform that ensured uninterrupted legal assistance, particularly during COVID19 lockdowns. Through this channel, 3,895 people (1,609 men and 2,450 women) were assisted remotely, which led to new capabilities among target groups: they could obtain realtime advice, triage their cases, and receive referrals without needing to travelcapabilities they did not have at the beginning of the intervention. Mobile Legal Aid Clinics (MLACs) expanded reach to underserved areas, with 1,743 clinics serving 20,102 people (7,095 men and 13,007 women). Court help desks6,720 sessions reaching 40,400 beneficiaries (13,442 men and 26,958 women)changed how users interacted with courts by demystifying procedures and accelerating access to remedies. Information centres (332 established) and widespread pamphlet distribution made rights information locally available, while mobile registration clinics assisted 2,387 people (955 men and 1,432 women) to secure identity documents, removing bureaucratic barriers to services and legal standing. These operations led to a replicable service delivery model, evidenced by adoption of the MLAC approach by state institutions, which changed institutional norms around bringing justice services to people rather than expecting people to come to justice. The difference is visible in seamless multichannel access, reduced travel and time costs, and sustained demand generation through communitylevel information points.
Building DutyBearer and Community Capacities LRFs targeted capacitybuilding initiatives produced notable behavioural and practice changes among key duty bearers. Police officers from the Victim Friendly Unit (VFU) adopted survivorcentred, rightsbased handling of sexual and genderbased violence cases, prioritizing medical evidence, confidentiality, and juvenile rights. ZPCS officers implemented gendersensitive and childfriendly practices, reforming infacility procedures and relations with inmates. Continuous collaboration with the National Prosecuting Authority improved case responsiveness, reduced backlogs, and strengthened institutional accountability. Traditional leaders, supported through training and monitoring, demonstrated improved procedural fairness and gender sensitivity in customary forums.
At the community level, operations led to broadbased capacity gains: 507 community paralegal trainings empowered 11,648 people (3,234 men and 6,298 women) with the skills to advise, refer, and document cases; 17 mentoring sessions strengthened 569 participants (193 men and 376 women); and 647 community dialogues engaged 19,888 people to collectively address local justice and servicedelivery concerns. These efforts changed attitudes and relations between citizens and local authorities, as trained volunteers and paralegals (including Community Rights and Responsibilities Promoters) fostered constructive engagement that resulted in practical improvements in waste management, road rehabilitation, and civil registration services. The target group is now capable of initiating rightsbased claims, documenting grievances, navigating referral pathways, and sustaining dialogue with duty bearerscapabilities that were limited or absent at programme inception. The difference is seen in the volume and quality of local problemsolving and the increased institutional responsiveness to communityraised issues.
Strengthening Citizen Agency and Participation The programme significantly strengthened citizen agency in justice processes. Through legal education and coaching, citizensespecially indigent litigantswere empowered to represent themselves effectively in court, with 20,854 people assisted as selfactors. This changed what individuals could do: they now prepare pleadings, understand evidentiary standards, meet procedural requirements, and present cases confidentlyreducing reliance on limited legal aid capacity and improving case throughput. Volunteer legal education sessions reached 154,444 people (56,475 men and 97,679 women), shifting communitylevel attitudes toward rights awareness and proactive problemsolving. LRFs documentation initiatives helped marginalized groups, including persons with disabilities and members of apostolic sects, acquire birth certificates and national identity documents through mobile registration clinics, enabling access to education, social protection, voting, and formal employment. These operations unequivocally made a difference by lowering barriers to entry into formal systems and increasing user confidence in courts and administrative bodies.
Advancing Gender Equality and Disability Inclusion The programme addressed structural inequalities affecting women, widows, and persons with disabilities by supporting alternative dispute resolution, mediation, and advocacy efforts that enabled rightsholders to reclaim land, property, and other entitlementsreducing householdlevel risk factors for genderbased violence and strengthening economic security. Disability rights education and advocacy contributed to the establishment of a Parliamentary Disability Caucus, while practical accessibility interventionssuch as wheelchair provision and improved courtroom facilitieschanged how persons with disabilities experience and navigate justice spaces. These measures led to attitudinal and relational shifts among justice actors and communities, fostering inclusion and reducing discrimination. Target groups are now better able to assert disability rights, access courts with fewer physical and procedural barriers, and mobilize institutional support when violations occurdemonstrating meaningful change at both individual and systemic levels.
Policy Reform, Strategic Litigation, and Accountability At the national level, LRFs strategic advocacy, policy engagement, and litigation efforts contributed to key legal reforms that enhanced rights protection. The organisation played a significant role in influencing the enactment of the Marriages Act (2022), which criminalized child marriage, and contributed to proposed amendments to the Criminal Law (Codification and Reform) Bill aimed at strengthening penalties for sexual offences. Through Access to Justice Working Groups, policy dialogues, and participation in regional and international forums, the programme facilitated reforms such as fee waivers for indigent litigants and formal recognition of paralegals in rural communities. Strategic litigation and 245 court monitoring sessions (covering civil and criminal matters), together with 83 traditional court monitoring sessions across 1,754 cases, improved judicial accountability and promoted consistent, rightsbased decisionmaking. These operations led to measurable shifts in policy and practicedemonstrating that advocacy combined with evidence from monitoring can change laws, institutional incentives, and courtroom behaviour. The difference is reflected in clearer protections, lower cost barriers, and stronger recognition of frontline paralegal work.
Challenges and Mitigation Despite its successes, the programme faced several operational, structural, and contextual challenges that required adaptive management. COVID19 disruptions (20202021): Restrictions severely limited mobility, disrupted court operations, and reduced inperson service provision. These constraints were mitigated through the rapid deployment of the tollfree call centre, remote legal assistance, and staggered MLACs aligned to public health protocols, ensuring continuity of services. Restrictive civic and regulatory environment: The programme operated within a constrained operating space for civil society, where periodic administrative hurdles, permissions for gatherings, and heightened scrutiny of community engagements occasionally slowed implementation and constrained public dialogue. LRF mitigated these challenges by strengthening compliance systems, maintaining transparent engagement with authorities at national and district levels, leveraging longstanding institutional relationships, and relying on communitybased structures (paralegals and volunteers) that could continue activities during periods of limited organisational mobility.
Partner capacity constraints: Resource limitations within the police, courts, and correctional services slowed case processing and referrals. LRF responded by enhancing coordination mechanisms, delivering targeted capacitybuilding, and instituting regular joint planning to harmonize expectations, referral pathways, and workflows.
Sociocultural resistance: Entrenched normsparticularly regarding gender roles and some customary practicesinitially hindered uptake of rightsbased approaches. Sustained engagement, mentorship, traditional court monitoring, and community dialogues gradually shifted attitudes, improving acceptance of humanrightsaligned procedures. Geographic barriers: Remoteness of target communities constrained early outreach. Expanded MLAC coverage, information centres, and collaboration with local volunteers widened reach and ensured continuity. By addressing these challenges through innovation, partnership, and contextresponsive strategies, the programme maintained momentum and ensured that institutional and communitylevel outcomes were not only achieved but sustained.
Conclusion The Access to Justice programme delivered systemic, transformative results that strengthened justice institutions, modernized service delivery, empowered communities, and improved legal protections for vulnerable groups. Operations led to sustained service availability across multiple channels, accelerated case resolution, and deeper institutional collaboration. Attitudes and behaviours among police, correctional officers, prosecutors, and traditional leaders shifted toward rightsbased norms, while relations between communities and local authorities became more constructive and accountabilityoriented. Target groups that were previously excluded or underserved are now able to navigate courts, assert rights, document grievances, and secure identity documents. The programme made a clear and demonstrable difference, evidenced by the breadth of reach, the number of cases resolved, the replication of models by state institutions, and the legal and policy reforms achievedadvancing fairness, equality, and the rule of law for all.
